subject: Physics
title: Magnetism and Matter
summary: A bar magnet behaves exactly like a current-carrying solenoid: both are magnetic dipoles with a magnetic moment m pointing from S to N.
The field of a magnetic dipole falls as 1/r³: on the axis it is twice as strong as on the equatorial line at the same distance, and the two fields point in opposite directions.
In a uniform field a dipole feels a torque τ = m × B (no net force) and has potential energy U = −m·B; it oscillates about the field direction like a compass needle.

Materials are diamagnetic (weakly repelled), paramagnetic (weakly attracted) or ferromagnetic (strongly attracted). Paramagnetism weakens with temperature (Curie's law); above the Curie temperature a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.

formulas.name: Magnetic moment
formulas.formula: bar magnet: m = q_m × 2l;  current loop/solenoid: m = N I A
formulas.note: Direction: S → N inside the magnet; for a loop use the right-hand rule.

formulas.name: Field on the axis of a dipole
formulas.when: Field along the magnet's axis (r ≫ length).

formulas.name: Field on the equatorial line
formulas.mistake: B_axial = 2 × B_equatorial at the same r — don't swap the factor 2.

formulas.name: Torque on a dipole
formulas.formula: τ = m × B;  |τ| = mB sin θ
formulas.note: Net force is zero in a uniform field — only torque acts.

formulas.name: Work to rotate a dipole
formulas.when: Turning a magnet in a field.

formulas.name: Oscillation of a magnet
formulas.when: Small oscillations of a magnet or compass needle in a uniform field.

formulas.name: Magnetisation and intensity
formulas.formula: M = m_net/V;  H = B₀/μ₀;  B = μ₀(H + M)

formulas.name: Susceptibility and permeability
formulas.formula: χ = M/H;  μ = μ₀(1 + χ);  μᵣ = 1 + χ
formulas.note: Diamagnets: χ small and negative; paramagnets: small positive; ferromagnets: very large positive.

formulas.name: Curie's law
formulas.note: Applies only to paramagnets; diamagnetism hardly depends on temperature.

formulas.name: Curie–Weiss law
formulas.formula: χ = C/(T − T_C) for T > T_C

examples.title: Axial field of a magnet
examples.problem: m = 0.5 A m². Field on the axis at 10 cm (μ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷)?

examples.title: Equatorial field
examples.problem: Same magnet, 10 cm on the equatorial line?
examples.solution: B = 10⁻⁷ × 0.5/(0.1)³ = 5 × 10⁻⁵ T — half the axial value.

examples.title: Torque on a magnet
examples.problem: m = 0.5 A m² at 30° to a 0.2 T field. Torque?

examples.title: Work to rotate
examples.problem: The same magnet is turned from 0° to 60°. Work needed?

examples.title: Solenoid as a magnet
examples.problem: A solenoid has 2000 turns, area 2 cm², current 1.5 A. Magnetic moment?

examples.title: Curie's law
examples.problem: A paramagnet has χ = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ at 300 K. χ at 400 K?

examples.title: Oscillating magnet

topics.title: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
topics.explain: Field lines of a bar magnet and of a solenoid look identical outside. Cutting a magnet in half gives two smaller magnets — isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist, unlike electric charges.

topics.title: Magnetic field lines
topics.explain: They form closed loops (outside N → S, inside S → N), never intersect, and are crowded where the field is strong. Gauss's law for magnetism: net flux through any closed surface is zero.

topics.title: Dipole in a uniform field
topics.explain: Stable equilibrium when m is along B (minimum energy), unstable when opposite. The torque tries to align m with B — this is how a compass works.

topics.title: Diamagnetic substances
topics.explain: Weakly repelled, move from stronger to weaker field; χ small negative (≈ −10⁻⁵). Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, water, nitrogen gas. Superconductors are perfect diamagnets (Meissner effect).

topics.title: Paramagnetic substances
topics.explain: Weakly attracted, move from weaker to stronger field; atoms have permanent moments that partly align. Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen gas, copper chloride. χ decreases as temperature rises.

topics.title: Ferromagnetic substances
topics.explain: Strongly attracted; domains align easily. Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium. Above the Curie temperature (Fe ≈ 1043 K) they become paramagnetic. Soft iron (easy to magnetise and demagnetise) is used in electromagnets and transformer cores; steel for permanent magnets.

topics.title: Syllabus note
topics.explain: Earth's magnetism (dip, declination, horizontal component) has been removed from the current NTA syllabus. Focus on dipole fields, torque and energy, and the three classes of materials with the effect of temperature.

ratta: τ = mB sinθ;  U = −mB cosθ;  W = mB(cosθ₁ − cosθ₂).
Dia: χ < 0;  para: small χ > 0;  ferro: huge χ.
Curie: χ = C/T (para);  ferro → para above T_C.
No magnetic monopoles; net flux through closed surface = 0.
